1. What is an Algorithm?
An algorithm is a sequence of unambiguous instructions for solving a problem — obtaining a required
output for any legitimate input in a finite amount of time.
Characteristics of an Algorithm:
Input: Zero or more quantities are externally supplied.
Output: At least one quantity is produced.
Definiteness: Each instruction must be clear, well-defined, and unambiguous.
Finiteness: Algorithm must terminate after a finite number of steps for all cases.
Efficiency: Every instruction must be basic enough to be carried out by hand.
Key Observations:
• The non-ambiguity requirement for each step cannot be compromised.
• The range of inputs must be specified carefully.
• The same algorithm can be represented in multiple ways.
• Several algorithms can solve the same problem — with different speeds and trade-offs.
Algorithm vs Program:
An algorithm terminates after a finite number of steps. A program does NOT have to satisfy this finiteness
condition — e.g., an operating system runs in a wait loop indefinitely.
Methods of Specifying an Algorithm:
Natural Language: Simple, easy to write but often ambiguous. Good for simple problems.
Flowchart: Graphic representation using connected geometric shapes. Good only for small, simple
algorithms.
Pseudocode: Combination of natural language and programming constructs. Most precise and
preferred method.

2. Algorithm Examples — Greatest Common Divisor (GCD)
The gcd(m, n) is the largest integer that divides both m and n evenly (with remainder zero). Three
methods are presented, each with different efficiency.
2.1. Middle-School Procedure
Informal / Inefficient
What it computes: gcd(m, n) via prime factorization.
Steps:
• Find prime factors of m.
• Find prime factors of n.
• Identify all common factors (if p appears p_m and p_n times, repeat min{p_m, p_n} times).
• Compute the product of all common factors — this is gcd(m, n).
Example: gcd(60, 24) = ?
60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 Common: 2 × 2 × 3 = 12
Limitation: Does not qualify as a legitimate algorithm in strict form — prime factorization steps are not
unambiguously defined (requires a list of primes). Step 3 is also unclear.
2.2. Consecutive Integer Checking Algorithm
Brute Force
What it computes: gcd(m, n) by checking all integers from min(m,n) down to 1.
Algorithm:
ALGORITHM ConsecGCD(m, n)
Step 1: t <- min{m, n}
Step 2: if m mod t = 0, go to Step 3; else go to Step 4
Step 3: if n mod t = 0, return t and stop; else go to Step 4
Step 4: t <- t - 1; go to Step 2
Basic Operation
Modulo division (m mod t, n mod t)
Efficiency
O(min(m, n)) — linear in the smaller value
Limitation
Does not work correctly if either input is 0
Example: gcd(60, 24): starts at t=24, tries 24,23,...,12. Returns 12.
2.3. Euclid's Algorithm
Decrease & Conquer
What it computes: gcd(m, n) using the property that gcd(m,n) = gcd(n, m mod n).
Algorithm:
ALGORITHM Euclid(m, n)
// Input: Two nonneg, not-both-zero integers m and n
// Output: Greatest common divisor of m and n
while n != 0 do
r <- m mod n

2.4. Sieve of Eratosthenes
Brute Force
What it computes: All prime numbers from 2 up to a given integer n > 1.
Algorithm:
ALGORITHM Sieve(n)
// Input: A positive integer n > 1
// Output: Array L of all primes <= n
for p <- 2 to n do A[p] <- p
for p <- 2 to floor(sqrt(n)) do
if A[p] != 0 // p not yet eliminated
j <- p * p
while j <= n do
A[j] <- 0 // mark composite
j <- j + p
return non-zero elements of A as L
Basic Operation
Marking composite: A[j] <- 0
Why start at p*p?
All smaller multiples (2p, 3p, ..., (p-1)p) already eliminated in earlier passes
Execution Count
~n ln(ln n) — from sum of reciprocals of primes up to sqrt(n)
Efficiency Class
O(n log log n)
Example: Primes up to 25: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23

3. Real-Life Algorithm Examples
3.1 Air Travel — Graph Problem
An airline network (Barbet Airlines) connects cities via directed flights. Some routes are one-way, some
bidirectional. The airline network is modeled as a directed graph where cities = nodes and flights =
edges.
Goals:
• Find all pairs of cities connected by any sequence of flights.
• Determine if travel from city A to city B is possible.
• Find the actual route from A to B.
Algorithmic questions raised:
• How does complexity scale with N (cities) and F (flights)?
• What data structure best represents the graph?
• Can we add constraints (time, cost) and still solve efficiently?
• What if we want cheapest or fastest route instead of just any route?
3.2 Xerox Shop — Scheduling Problem
Jobs with known page counts and deadlines need to be scheduled on photocopiers to maximize on-time
deliveries (minimize discounts given for late jobs).
Approaches considered:
Brute Force: Try every permutation of jobs. Exponential — impractical for even 30 jobs.
Decomposition: Recursively pick best first job, then solve for remaining n-1 jobs.
Greedy: Always pick the "best" next job by some criterion (shortest job, closest deadline) without
backtracking.
3.3 Document Similarity — Edit Distance
Edit distance is the minimum number of single-character operations (insert, delete, replace) needed to
transform one document into another. Used for plagiarism detection, code diff tools, and web search result
grouping.
Solution approaches:
• Brute Force: Try all delete/insert sequences — very inefficient.
• Recursion: Match first characters, then recurse on rest — naive recursion is inefficient (overlapping
subproblems).
• Dynamic Programming: Solve each subproblem once, store results in a table. Efficient O(mn)
solution.

4. Types of Algorithms
4.1 Brute Force / Exhaustive Search
Directly based on problem definition. Tries all possibilities.
Examples: Consecutive Integer GCD • Bubble Sort, Selection Sort • Sequential Search • String Matching (Naive)
Typical Efficiency: O(n²) to O(n!) depending on problem
4.2 Recursive Algorithm
Solves problem by calling itself on smaller subproblems with a base condition.
Examples: Factorial n! • Fibonacci numbers • Tower of Hanoi • DFS for Graphs
Typical Efficiency: Varies — depends on recurrence relation
4.3 Divide and Conquer
Divide into smaller instances, solve recursively, combine solutions.
Examples: Merge Sort • Quick Sort • Strassen's Matrix Multiplication • Binary Search
Typical Efficiency: Often O(n log n)
4.4 Decrease and Conquer
Reduce input size at each step (not split — just reduce).
Examples: Binary Search • Euclid's Algorithm • Finding min/max element
Typical Efficiency: Often O(log n)
4.5 Transform and Conquer
Transform problem to easier form, then solve. Three variants: instance simplification, representation
change, problem reduction.
Examples: Data compression • Machine learning preprocessing • Image processing
Typical Efficiency: Varies
4.6 Dynamic Programming
Solve overlapping subproblems once, store results in a table (memoization/tabulation).
Examples: Fibonacci (tabulated) • Knapsack Problem • Floyd-Warshall • Edit Distance
Typical Efficiency: Usually polynomial — O(n²) or O(nm)
4.7 Greedy Algorithm
Build solution step-by-step: each step must be feasible, locally optimal, and irrevocable.
Examples: Dijkstra Shortest Path • Prim's MST • Kruskal's MST • Huffman Coding
Typical Efficiency: Often O(n log n)
4.8 Backtracking
Incrementally build solution; abandon (backtrack) paths that violate constraints.
Examples: N-Queens Problem • Hamiltonian Cycle • Rat in Maze • M-Coloring
Typical Efficiency: Exponential in worst case

5. Performance Analysis Framework
Two Kinds of Efficiency:
• Time Complexity (TC): How fast the algorithm runs — measured by counting basic operations.
• Space Complexity (SC): How much extra memory the algorithm uses beyond its input/output.
Running Time Formula:
T(n) ≈ cop × C(n)
Where: n = input size, c_op = execution time of basic operation, C(n) = number of times basic operation
executes.

6. Asymptotic Notations
Big-O Notation O(g(n))
Definition: Upper bound. t(n) ∈ O(g(n)) if there exist c > 0 and nI ≥ 0 such that t(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ nI.
Informal meaning: "t(n) grows no faster than g(n)" — set of all functions with same or lower order of growth.
Proofs / Examples:
• P1: 100n + 5 ∈ O(n²): since 100n+5 ≤ 101n ≤ 101n² for n≥2. Use c=101, nI=2.
• P2: 100n + 5 ∈ O(n): since 100n+5 ≤ 101n for n≥5. Use c=101, nI=5.
• P3: 100n²+5n+2 ∈ O(n²): since 100n²+5n+2 ≤ 101n² for n≥6. Use c=101, nI=6.
C-value trick: Trick: If T(n) has +, add 1 to leading coefficient for c. If -, use leading coefficient as c.
Omega Notation Ω(g(n))
Definition: Lower bound. t(n) ∈ Ω(g(n)) if there exist c > 0 and nI ≥ 0 such that t(n) ≥ c·g(n) for all n ≥ nI.
Informal meaning: "t(n) grows at least as fast as g(n)" — set of all functions with same or higher order of growth.
Proofs / Examples:
• P4: n³ ∈ Ω(n²): since n³ ≥ 1·n² for all n≥0. Use c=1, nI=0.
• P5: ¹⁄In(n-1) ∈ Ω(n²): since ¹⁄In² - ¹⁄In ≥ ¹⁄In² for n≥2. Use c=1/4, nI=2.
• P6: 5n²+n ∈ Ω(n²): since 5n²+n ≥ 5n² for all n≥0. Use c=5, nI=0.
C-value trick: Trick: If T(n) has +, use leading coefficient as c. If -, use a smaller value than leading coefficient.
Theta Notation Θ(g(n))
Definition: t(n) ∈ Θ(g(n)) if there exist cI,cI > 0 and nI ≥ 0 such that cIg(n) ≤ t(n) ≤ cIg(n) for all n ≥
nI.
Informal meaning: "t(n) has exactly the same order of growth as g(n)" — tight bound (both O and Ω).
Proofs / Examples:
• P7: ¹⁄In(n-1) ∈ Θ(n²): Upper: ¹⁄In²-¹⁄In ≤ ¹⁄In², so cI=¹⁄I. Lower: ¹⁄In²-¹⁄In ≥ ¹⁄In² for n≥2, so
cI=¹⁄I. Select nI=2.
• P8: 100n+5 ∈ Θ(n): Lower cI=100 (n≥1), Upper cI=101 (n≥5). Select nI=5.
C-value trick: A function is Θ(g) if and only if it is both O(g) and Ω(g).
6.1 Useful Property (Sum Rule):
If tI(n) ∈ O(gI(n)) and tI(n) ∈ O(gI(n)), then tI(n)+tI(n) ∈ O(max{gI(n), gI(n)}).
This means the overall efficiency of an algorithm with two consecutive parts is determined by the slower
part.
6.2 Limit Method for Comparing Orders of Growth:
lim [t(n) / g(n)] as n -> infinity:
= 0 => t(n) has SMALLER order of growth than g(n) => t(n) in O(g(n))
= c > 0 => t(n) has SAME order of growth as g(n) => t(n) in Theta(g(n))
= inf => t(n) has LARGER order of growth than g(n) => t(n) in Omega(g(n))

Useful tools: L'Hospital's rule: lim t(n)/g(n) = lim t'(n)/g'(n) | Stirling's formula: n! ≈ sqrt(2πn) × (n/e)I
Example P9: Compare ¹⁄In(n-1) and n²: lim [¹⁄In² - ¹⁄In] / n² = 1/2. Since c=1/2 (constant) ⇒ Θ(n²).
Example P10: Compare logIn and sqrt(n): limit = 0 ⇒ logIn grows slower than sqrt(n). logIn ∈
o(sqrt(n)).

7. Mathematical Analysis of Non-Recursive Algorithms
General Plan (5 steps):
Step 1: Decide on a parameter n indicating input size.
Step 2: Identify the basic operation (usually in the innermost loop).
Step 3: Check if count depends only on n, or also on specifics — if latter, analyze cases separately.
Step 4: Set up a sum expressing the number of times basic operation executes.
Step 5: Use summation formulas/rules to find closed-form or order of growth.
Key Summation Formulas:
• Σ(i from l to u) c·aI = c × ΣaI (R1: constant factor rule)
• Σ(i from l to u) 1 = u - l + 1 (S1: count of terms)
• Σ(i from 1 to n) i = n(n+1)/2 ≈ ¹⁄In² ∈ Θ(n²) (S2: sum of first n integers)
7.1. Max Element
Linear
Computes: Largest value in array A[0..n-1] of real numbers.
Algorithm:
ALGORITHM MaxElement(A[0..n-1])
// Input: Array A[0..n-1] of real numbers
// Output: Value of largest element
maxval <- A[0]
for i <- 1 to n-1 do
if A[i] > maxval
maxval <- A[i]
return maxval
Basic Operation
Comparison: A[i] > maxval
Execution Count
C(n) = Σ(i=1 to n-1) 1 = n-1
Efficiency Class
Θ(n)
No case distinction — comparison runs exactly n-1 times regardless of array content.

Quadratic

Algorithm:
ALGORITHM UniqueElements(A[0..n-1])
// Input: Array A[0..n-1]
// Output: true if all distinct, false otherwise
for i <- 0 to n-2 do

7.3. Matrix Multiplication
Cubic
Computes: Product C = A×B of two n×n matrices, where C[i,j] = Σ A[i,k]×B[k,j].
Algorithm:
ALGORITHM MatrixMultiplication(A, B)
// Input: Two n x n matrices A and B
// Output: Matrix C = AB
for i <- 0 to n-1 do
for j <- 0 to n-1 do
C[i,j] <- 0
for k <- 0 to n-1 do
C[i,j] <- C[i,j] + A[i,k] * B[k,j]
return C
Basic Operation
Multiplication: A[i,k] * B[k,j]
Execution Count
M(n) = ΣIΣIΣI 1 = n³
Efficiency Class
Θ(n³)
Count depends only on n. No case distinction. T(n) ≈ (c_m + c_a)×n³.

8. Sorting Algorithms (Brute Force)
8.1. Selection Sort
Brute Force / Sorting
Computes: Sorts array A[0..n-1] in non-decreasing order by repeatedly selecting the minimum from the
unsorted tail.
Working: On pass i (0 to n-2), find minimum in A[i..n-1] and swap it with A[i]. After n-1 passes, array is
sorted.
Algorithm:
ALGORITHM SelectionSort(A[0..n-1])
// Input: Array A[0..n-1] of orderable elements
// Output: Array sorted in nondecreasing order
for i <- 0 to n-2 do
min <- i
for j <- i+1 to n-1 do
if A[j] < A[min] min <- j
swap A[i] and A[min]
Basic Operation
Key comparison: A[j] < A[min]
Execution Count
C(n) = Σ(i=0 to n-2)(n-1-i) = (n-1)n/2 ≈ ¹⁄In² ∈ Θ(n²)
Key Swaps
Exactly n-1 swaps — one per outer loop iteration. This is Θ(n), much better than
bubble sort!

Comparison count is input-independent.

Same (n-1)n/2 comparisons regardless of order.

8.2. Bubble Sort
Brute Force / Sorting

— 15 —
CS252 DAA | Module 1
Dr. Josephine Prem Kumar | CIT 2025-26
Computes: Sorts array A[0..n-1] in non-decreasing order by repeatedly swapping adjacent out-of-order
pairs.
Working: Each pass "bubbles up" the largest unsorted element to its final position. After n-1 passes, array
is sorted.
Algorithm:
ALGORITHM BubbleSort(A[0..n-1])
// Input: Array A[0..n-1] of orderable elements
// Output: Array sorted in nondecreasing order
for i <- 0 to n-2 do
for j <- 0 to n-2-i do
if A[j+1] < A[j]
swap A[j] and A[j+1]
Basic Operation
Key comparison: A[j+1] < A[j]
Execution Count
C(n) = Σ(i=0 to n-2)(n-1-i) = (n-1)n/2 ≈ ¹⁄In² ∈ Θ(n²)
Key Swaps (worst)
S_worst(n) = (n-1)n/2 ∈ Θ(n²) — reverse sorted input
Optimization
If a pass makes no swaps, array is sorted — stop early. Best case becomes Θ(n).
Case
Complexity
Description
Best
Θ(n) (optimized)
Already sorted — 0 swaps, one pass detects this (optimized version).
Average
Θ(n²)
Quadratic comparisons and swaps on average.
Worst
Θ(n²)
Reverse-sorted — maximum swaps = maximum comparisons.

9. Searching Algorithms (Brute Force)
9.1. Sequential Search
Brute Force / Search
Computes: Index of first element in A[0..n-1] equal to key K, or -1 if not found.
Algorithm:
ALGORITHM SequentialSearch(A[0..n-1], K)
// Input: Array A[0..n-1] and search key K
// Output: Index of first match, or -1
i <- 0
while i < n and A[i] != K do
i <- i + 1
if i < n return i
else return -1
Basic Operation
Comparison: A[i] != K
Average Case
Formula
C_avg(n) = p(n+1)/2 + n(1-p), where p = P(successful search)
If p=1 (must find)
C_avg = (n+1)/2 — inspects ~half the list on average
If p=0 (never finds)
C_avg = n — inspects all elements
Case
Complexity
Description
Best
C_best = 1
First element equals K.
Average
C_avg = p(n+1)/2
+ n(1-p)
Probabilistic average over all inputs.
Worst
C_worst = n
K not in list, or last element matches.
9.2. Brute-Force String Matching
Brute Force / Search
Computes: Index i of first occurrence of pattern P[0..m-1] in text T[0..n-1], or -1 if not found.
Working: Align pattern at each position i in text. Compare characters left to right. On mismatch, shift
pattern one position right.
Algorithm:
ALGORITHM BruteForceStringMatch(T[0..n-1], P[0..m-1])
// Input: Text T (n chars) and Pattern P (m chars)
// Output: Index of first match, or -1
for i <- 0 to n-m do
j <- 0

j <- j + 1
if j = m return i
return -1

Character comparison: P[j] = T[i+j]

m(n-m+1) comparisons — all m chars match before mismatch at each of n-m+1

10. Mathematical Analysis of Recursive Algorithms
General Plan for Recursive Analysis (5 steps):
Step 1: Decide on parameter n indicating input size.
Step 2: Identify the basic operation.
Step 3: Check if count varies on different inputs of same size — if so, analyze cases separately.
Step 4: Set up a recurrence relation with initial condition for basic operation count.
Step 5: Solve the recurrence (backward substitution, or ascertain order of growth).
Backward Substitution Method: Repeatedly substitute the recurrence into itself to find a pattern, then
express as a closed-form formula.
10.1. Recursive Factorial
Recursive / Linear
Computes: F(n) = n! = n × (n-1) × ... × 1, with F(0) = 1.
Algorithm:
ALGORITHM F(n)
// Input: Nonneg integer n
// Output: Value of n!
if n = 0 return 1
else return F(n-1) * n
Basic Operation
Multiplication: F(n-1) × n
Recurrence
M(n) = M(n-1) + 1, M(0) = 0
Solution (Backward
Sub)
M(n) = M(n-1)+1 = M(n-2)+2 = ... = M(0)+n = n. Exactly n multiplications for input n.
Efficiency Class
Θ(n)
No case distinction. Iterative version needs same n multiplications without recursion overhead.
10.2. Tower of Hanoi
Recursive / Exponential
Computes: Sequence of n disk moves: transfer n disks from peg 1 to peg 3 using peg 2 as auxiliary. Rule:
never place larger disk on smaller.
Algorithm:
ALGORITHM Hanoi(n, Source, Dest, Temp)
if n = 1
print "Move disk 1 from Source to Dest"
return
Hanoi(n-1, Source, Temp, Dest) // move n-1 to temp
print "Move disk n from Source to Dest"

10.3. Binary Digits Count (Recursive)
Recursive / Logarithmic
Computes: Number of bits in binary representation of positive decimal integer n.
Algorithm:
ALGORITHM BinRec(n)
// Input: Positive decimal integer n
// Output: Number of binary digits in n
if n = 1 return 1
else return BinRec(floor(n/2)) + 1
Basic Operation
Addition: BinRec(floor(n/2)) + 1
Recurrence
A(n) = A(floor(n/2)) + 1, A(1) = 0 For n = 2^k: A(2^k) = A(2^(k-1)) + 1
Solution (Backward
Sub)
A(2^k) = A(2^(k-1))+1 = A(2^(k-2))+2 = ... = A(2^0)+k = k Since n = 2^k => k =
logIn A(n) = logIn = floor(logIn)
Efficiency Class
Θ(log n)
Recurrence has floor(n/2) — only solvable exactly for n = 2^k. Solution generalizes to all n via floor.
